lessons.title: Characteristics used to classify domestic animals

pages.body:
Think about your home or community. Chickens scratching in a yard, a goat tied near a house, a cow grazing in a field. These are all domestic animals, animals that people keep and care for.

- List as many domestic animals as you can think of from your community.
- For each one, think about what it eats and how big it is.

A domestic animal is an animal that has been tamed and is kept and cared for by people, usually for food, work or other benefits.

pages.title: Characteristics used to classify domestic animals
pages.body:
Domestic animals can be sorted into groups using several characteristics that you can observe directly.

| **Characteristic** | **What to look at** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | The general body shape and features, such as horns, a hump, or a beak | A cow has horns and a hump. A chicken has a beak and feathers instead of fur. |
| Colour | The colour or pattern of the skin, fur or feathers | Goats may be white, brown, black or spotted. |
| Size | How big or small the animal is, including its height and weight | A cow is much larger than a chicken or a rabbit. |
| Feeding habits | What the animal eats and how it feeds | A goat browses on leaves and shrubs. A pig eats both plants and food scraps. |

questions.q: List and discuss three characteristics, other than digestive system, that could be used to classify domestic animals.

parts.a: Shape (body shape and features such as horns or a beak), colour (of skin, fur or feathers), size (height and weight) and feeding habits (what the animal eats).

pages.title: Breeds of domestic animals
pages.body: Within one kind of animal, such as cattle or goats, there are different breeds. A breed is a particular type of an animal species, developed to have certain features, such as fast growth, high milk yield, or the ability to survive well in the local climate.

| **Animal** | **Example breeds found in Ghana** |
|---|---|
| Cattle | West African Shorthorn (a small, hardy local breed) and White Fulani or Zebu (a larger breed with a hump, kept mainly in the north) |
| Sheep | West African Dwarf sheep, also called Djallonke (small, hardy, the most common local breed) and Sahelian sheep (a larger breed) |
| Goats | West African Dwarf goat (small, hardy, the most common local breed) |
| Pigs | Local pigs, and exotic breeds such as Large White and Landrace, kept mainly on commercial farms |
| Poultry (chickens) | Local (indigenous) fowl, hardy but lower egg and meat yield, and exotic breeds such as Leghorn (eggs) and Rhode Island Red (eggs and meat) |

> **DEFINITION** **Breed:** a particular type of a domestic animal species, developed or recognised for certain features such as size, colour or productivity.

Another useful way to classify domestic animals is by looking at their digestive system, which is closely linked to what and how they eat. Using this approach, domestic animals fall into three main groups.

questions.q: Name one breed of cattle, one breed of sheep, and one breed of goat found in Ghana.

parts.a: Cattle: West African Shorthorn or White Fulani (Zebu). Sheep: West African Dwarf (Djallonke) or Sahelian. Goat: West African Dwarf.

ideas.t: A cattle breed: West African Shorthorn or White Fulani (Zebu)
A sheep breed: West African Dwarf (Djallonke) or Sahelian
A goat breed: West African Dwarf goat

questions.q: What is a breed? Give one example of a breed of cattle found in Ghana.

parts.a: A breed is a particular type of an animal species developed for certain features such as size, colour or productivity. An example is the West African Shorthorn.

ideas.t: A particular type of an animal species with certain features
Example of a cattle breed: West African Shorthorn or White Fulani (Zebu)

pages.body:
| **Group** | **Digestive system** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|
| Ruminants | A stomach with four chambers. They swallow plant food, then bring it back up to chew again as cud, before it is fully digested. | Cattle, goats, sheep |
| Monogastrics | A single, simple stomach, similar in principle to a human stomach. Some monogastrics eat only plants (monogastric herbivores, such as rabbits and horses), while others eat both plants and meat. | Pigs, rabbits, horses |
| Poultry | No teeth or true stomach in the same sense. A crop stores swallowed food, and a muscular gizzard grinds it, often with the help of tiny stones the bird has swallowed. | Chickens, ducks, turkeys, guinea fowl |

> **DEFINITION** **Ruminant:** a domestic animal with a four chambered stomach that chews its food again as cud after first swallowing it. **Monogastric:** a domestic animal with a single, simple stomach. **Poultry:** domestic birds kept for their eggs, meat or feathers.

> **Not every monogastric animal eats meat. Rabbits and horses have a single stomach but eat only plants, so they are called monogastric herbivores.**

parts.a: It is most likely a ruminant, because ruminants swallow their food and bring it back up to chew again as cud.

parts.a: Birds have no teeth. They swallow their food into a crop, which stores it, and then a muscular gizzard grinds it, often helped by tiny stones the bird has swallowed.

pages.body:
A family keeps three chickens in their backyard. A large farm nearby keeps thousands of chickens and sells eggs to shops across the region. Both are keeping the same kind of animal, but for different reasons.

- Why do you think the family keeps their chickens?
- Why do you think the large farm keeps its chickens?

People keep domestic animals for two main purposes. When an animal or its products are used within the household, this is domestic use. When an animal or its products are raised and sold for profit, this is commercial use. The same animal can serve both purposes, depending on how it is kept and used.

> **DEFINITION** **Domestic use:** keeping and using an animal or its products mainly to meet the needs of a household. **Commercial use:** raising an animal and selling it, or its products, to earn money. **By-product:** a useful material obtained from an animal in addition to its main product, such as manure, hide or bones.

**Ruminants and monogastrics**
- Meat, for food.
- Milk, mainly from ruminants such as cattle and goats.
- Hides and skins, used to make leather.
- Draught power, such as cattle used to plough farmland or pull carts.
- Manure, an organic nutrient source for crops.

**Poultry**
- Eggs, for food and for sale.
- Meat, for food.
- Feathers, used in some crafts and products.
- Droppings, an organic nutrient source for crops.

Notice that manure and droppings appear as by-products for both groups. This connects directly to what you learned about organic nutrient sources. Animal waste is a valuable resource, not simply waste to be thrown away.

> **The same animal can have both a domestic use and a commercial use. A farmer's cow may provide milk for the family and also be sold at market.**

questions.q: Explain the difference between domestic use and commercial use, using an example of each.

parts.a: Domestic use means keeping an animal or its products for the needs of the household, for example eggs eaten at home. Commercial use means raising and selling it for profit, for example selling eggs at the market.

ideas.t: Domestic use: kept or used for the needs of the household
Commercial use: raised and sold to earn money

questions.q: Name three by-products of domestic animals, and state one use for each.

parts.a: Manure (an organic nutrient source for crops), hides and skins (leather), poultry droppings (organic nutrient source), feathers (crafts), bones.

questions.q: Choose two domestic animals from your community. Describe the domestic and commercial uses of each.

parts.a: For example, a cow gives milk for the family (domestic use) and can be sold at market (commercial use); chickens give eggs for the home and eggs and meat that are sold.

ideas.t: Describes a commercial use (selling for profit)

questions.q: Name three by-products of domestic animals.

parts.a: Manure, hides and skins, droppings, feathers or bones.

questions.q: A family keeps two goats for milk and meat at home, and also sells goat manure to a nearby crop farmer. Identify the domestic use, the commercial use, and the by-product in this example.

parts.a: Domestic use: the milk and meat for the family. Commercial use: selling the goat manure to the crop farmer. By-product: the manure.

ideas.t: Domestic use: milk and meat for the family

questions.q: Think about everything you have learned about domestic animals.

parts.q: Describe the three groups used to classify domestic animals, based on their digestive systems.
parts.a: Ruminants have a four-chambered stomach and chew cud. Monogastrics have a single, simple stomach. Poultry have no true stomach; they use a crop to store food and a gizzard to grind it.

ideas.t: Poultry: crop and gizzard, no teeth

parts.q: Give two examples of animals in each group.
parts.a: Ruminants: cattle, goats, sheep. Monogastrics: pigs, rabbits, horses. Poultry: chickens, ducks, turkeys, guinea fowl.

ideas.t: Two poultry birds (chickens, ducks, turkeys, guinea fowl)

parts.q: Explain the difference between domestic use and commercial use, with an example of each.
parts.a: Domestic use means using the animal or its products for the household, for example eggs eaten at home. Commercial use means raising and selling them for profit, for example selling eggs.

ideas.t: Domestic use: kept or used for the needs of the household
Commercial use: raised and sold to earn money

parts.q: Explain why animal manure and droppings are valuable by-products, linking your answer to what you know about plant nutrients.
parts.a: Manure and droppings are organic nutrient sources that supply nutrients to crops, so animal waste is a valuable resource and not simply waste.

ideas.t: They are organic nutrient sources for crops
Animal waste is a valuable resource, not to be thrown away

pages.body:
- A domestic animal is an animal that has been tamed and is kept and cared for by people.
- Domestic animals can be classified by shape, colour, size and feeding habits.
- A breed is a particular type of a domestic animal species, such as the West African Shorthorn breed of cattle or the West African Dwarf breed of sheep and goats.
- Ruminants have a four chambered stomach and chew cud. Examples are cattle, goats and sheep.
- Monogastrics have a single, simple stomach. Some are herbivores, such as rabbits and horses, while others eat both plants and meat.
- Poultry are domestic birds with no true stomach in the same sense. They use a crop and a gizzard to store and grind food.
- Domestic use means keeping an animal mainly to meet household needs. Commercial use means raising and selling an animal or its products for profit.
- Domestic animals provide meat, milk, eggs, hides, draught power, feathers and manure, among other by-products.

| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Domestic animal | An animal that has been tamed and is kept and cared for by people |
| Breed | A particular type of a domestic animal species, developed or recognised for certain features |
| Ruminant | A domestic animal with a four chambered stomach that chews its food again as cud |
| Monogastric | A domestic animal with a single, simple stomach |
| Monogastric herbivore | A monogastric animal that eats only plants, such as a rabbit or horse |
| Poultry | Domestic birds kept for their eggs, meat or feathers |
| Cud | Partly digested food that a ruminant brings back up from its stomach to chew again |
| Domestic use | Keeping and using an animal or its products mainly for household needs |
| Commercial use | Raising and selling an animal or its products to earn money |
| By-product | A useful material obtained from an animal in addition to its main product |
